newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn's Lafontaine- Upper house will quash tax bill.
newsitem.headline: Bonn's Lafontaine- Upper house will quash tax bill.

text.p: Oskar Lafontaine, leader of Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD), is certain that a bill aiming to reform the nation's tax and pension systems will be rejected by the Bundesrat upper house of parliament.

In an interview with Germany's Berliner Tageszeitung newspaper due to be published on Friday, Lafontaine lashed out at 'tax breaks for the rich' and said no state represented in the SPD-dominated Bundesrat would agree to the plans of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition.
Lafontaine said that he was prepared to seek a compromise with the government, but said: "Tax giveaways of between 20,000 and 100,000 marks for the top 10,000 (earners) are shameless".
Even ministers within Kohl's Christian Democrat (CDU) party had admitted that the tax reform bill would not help to boost tax revenues, he told the newspaper.

Latest figures show tax revenues were were down 4.3 percent in the first quarter of this year in comparision with a year earlier, a worrying issue for Finance Minister Theo Waigel who is keen to ensure Germany meets the entry criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

The government plans, the bulk of which would not filter through until 1999, aim to cut taxes by around 30 billion marks in the next two years with a package that includes a proposal to slash the top 53 percent rate of income tax.
But Lafontaine called this proposal "the third edition of the tax lie".
Seperately, Lafontaine told a mass May Day union rally in Leipzig that any tax cuts could only be moderate.
"A reduction in taxes is only possible to a modest degree," he said, adding that an overall tax cut of about 2,000 marks a year for the average family was possible given current state finances.
He said government promises of substantial tax cuts were untrue, and urged opposition to the plans. "Don't believe these promises," he told thousands of demonstrators.
Negotiations between the SPD and the coalition on tax reform failed last week, with Lafontaine accusing the government of trying to introduce a "reform against the people and against the economy".

But the tax battle has also highlighted rifts within the SPD opposition, with Lafontaine, seen as the hardliner, pitched against the more dovish Gerhard Schroeder, who has repeatedly called for compromise.
Speculation is rife that Schroeder will challenge Lafontaine for the right to stand as the SPD candidate against Kohl in the October 1998 general elections.

The bill is now due to go to the Bundesrat, where many independent analysts expect it to be rejected, and must then wait until September when a mediation committee will attempt to hammer out a compromise between the two sides.
On Monday, Chancellor Kohl repeated an invitation to the SPD to return to the negotiating table to discuss the reforms.
